children.html: Relationships of Goal Orientation, Metacognitive Activity, and Practice Strategies With Learning Outcomes and Transfer
J. Kevin Ford Michigan State University
Daniel A. Weissbein Michigan State University
Stanley M. Gully George Mason University

A model of learning transfer that focused on the active role of the learner was developed and tested within a complex decision-making task. The study examined how individual differences, learning strategies, and training outcomes influenced transfer of learning to a more complex task. A sample of 93 undergraduate students participated in a 2-day radar operations study. Hierarchical regression analysis results indicated that mastery orientation was positively related to metacognitive activity of the learner. Metacognitive activity was significantly related to knowledge acquisition, skilled performance at the end of training, and self-efficacy. All 3 of these training outcomes were related to performance on the transfer task. Implications of these findings for research and practice are discussed.

Learning and transfer are critical outcomes for any training program. Individuals must acquire knowledge, skills, and attitudes and then apply these capabilities to other contexts. Two important factors that impact learning and transfer outcomes are trainee characteristics and training design elements (Baldwin & Ford, 1988). Research on trainee characteristics has focused rather narrowly on cognitive ability, motivation to leam, and demographic variables such as level of education. Yet, although research on trainee characteristics has expanded in recent
years (Baldwin & Magjuka, 1997), less attention has been paid to the role of the learner within the learning process.

In contrast, the instructional psychology literature has been quite interested in the proactive nature of the learner (Smith, Ford, & Kozlowski, 1997). One emerging area is the examination of the learning or goal orientation of the learner and how that impacts an individual's approach to a learning task. A second area concerns the learning strategies that individuals apply within a learning setting to meet objectives.

The majority of training design research has taken a behaviorist approach to the study of learning principles such as overlearning, schedules of reinforcement, and conditions of practice. These principles treat the learner as a "black box" who is acted upon by instructional design factors. Researchers have begun to call for a perspective that integrates design parameters with the cognitive processing of the learner (e.g., Goldstein, 1991, 1993; Howell & Cooke, 1989; R. A. Schmidt & Bjork, 1992; Tannenbaum & Yukl, 1992). One area of interest is the extent to which the training design provides the learner with some level of control over the learning process (Ford & Kraiger, 1995).

The present study expands upon training research in three ways. First, it focuses on a learning environment that requires the active participation of the trainee. Individuals can structure and guide their own learning pro-

Second, this study draws on the theoretical work in cognitive and instructional psychology to identify individual differences and learning strategies and to test how these factors are related to learning outcomes and transfer to a more complex task. Third, this study takes a multidimensional perspective to learning. It examines both how trainee characteristics and training design factors are related to knowledge, skill, and affective learning outcomes, and the linkage of these outcomes to training transfer (Kraiger, Ford, & Salas, 1993). These training issues are explored within a complex, decision-making task in which individuals must combine multiple pieces of information and prioritize their actions.

Traditional training design principles provide a structured and sequenced environment for mastering training content. For example, design principles suggest that correct behavior should be reinforced, that training exercises should proceed from simple to complex, and that feedback should be provided that is frequent and specific (Baldwin & Ford, 1988). R. A. Schmidt and Bjork (1992), though, illustrate how these traditional design principles may foster short-term learning and immediate retention but may not transfer to more complex task situations.
Researchers in cognitive and instructional psychology have begun to examine learning environments that facili-

tate learning and transfer by taking into account individual needs and preferences of learners. Learner control is a construct now being actively investigated in the computer assisted instruction and intelligent tutoring systems literature, but it pertains to other instructional methods as well (Ford & Kraiger, 1995). Learner control refers to the extent to which trainees have the opportunity to select the method, timing, practice, or feedback, or all four portions of training (Milheim & Martin, 1991). With greater control, learners can more actively tailor the training to meet their own changing needs. It is suggested that this method for engaging learners more actively during training leads them to learn the deeper, structural elements of the task more effectively.

In the present study, learners are placed in a training environment in which they choose the complexity of the exercises they practice. The purpose of this study is to examine how individual differences in goal orientation, metacognitive activity, and practice strategies are related to learning and transfer outcomes when individuals have control and choice of their practice exercises. The model to be examined is presented in Figure 1. The model presents hypothesized linkages among individual differences, learning strategies, learning outcomes, and training transfer. Figure 1 depicts a learning process in which the characteristics an individual brings to the training context are related to how they approach the learning task. These learning strategies are then related to what is learned from

training, which in turn relates the training transfer to a more complex task. Although the figure depicts an integrated model, it contains specific relationships between individual differences, learning strategies, learning outcomes, and transfer. Implicit in this model is that the relationships between specific variables are expected to be found after controlling for factors that occur prior to (or concurrent with) them in the learning process. The following sections describe the specific hypotheses embedded in this overall process model.

Kraiger et al. (1993) argued that the training literature has taken a narrow focus on learning. They presented a typology that conceptualized learning as a multidimensional construct, identifying three primary types of learning outcomes: knowledge, skills, and affect. Although the three types of outcomes are linked in complex ways (see Kraiger et al., 1993; Quinones, Ford, Sego, & Smith, 1995), the present study investigates how individual difference factors and learning strategies are related to these three types of learning outcomes. First, it examines the acquisition of the necessary declarative and procedural knowledge for performing a complex, decision-making task. Second, it examines the skills that lead to proficient task performance. Finally, the study identifies the factors that lead individuals to develop greater self-efficacy for successfully handling task demands (Bandura, 1982).

This research also focuses on how the three learning outcomes are related to transfer performance. Training should prepare individuals to apply what was learned to more complex situations than were experienced during training (Baldwin & Ford, 1988; Goldstein, 1993; R. A. Schmidt & Bjork, 1992). To achieve transfer, one must have a sufficient knowledge base to recognize what is required in the transfer environment (Glaser, 1986). Critical task skills must be proceduralized into more efficient and elegant task routines so as to improve task performance (e.g., Anderson, 1982). Finally, self-efficacy must be enhanced as individuals with greater confidence in their task capabilities are more resilient to the difficulties faced when trying to apply their knowledge and skills (Bandura & Wood, 1989). It is hypothesized that knowledge, skills, and self-efficacy are positively related to transfer performance.

In instructional psychology, the shift to a cognitive perspective on learning has led to an interest in the strategies used by individuals to learn training material. Learning strategies are defined as the behaviors or thoughts that a learner engages in during learning and that affect the

learner's encoding, storage, organization, and retrieval of knowledge (Weinstein & Mayer, 1986). Learning strategies have been examined in terms of higher order metacognitive control over learning, as well as practice strategies that are applied directly to the learning materials.

Metacognition is defined as an individual's knowledge of and control over his or her cognitions (Flavell, 1979). Metacognition includes planning, monitoring, and revising goal appropriate behavior (Brown, Bransford, Ferrara, & Campione, 1983). Individuals with greater metacognitive skills are expected to learn more effectively because they monitor their progress, determine when they are having problems, and adjust their learning accordingly.

Kanfer and Ackerman (1989) suggested that self-regulatory activities that result from setting difficult goals may inhibit skilled performance early in the skill acquisition process, as they take up cognitive resources that could best be used for learning the task and performing. Earley, Connolly, and Ekegren (1989), though, contend that setting difficult performance goals for complex tasks induces pressures to perform, yielding ineffective strategy search and selection. Thus, they contended that ineffective strategy search, selection, monitoring, and evaluation processes are the source of the skill acquisition and performance problems.

We agree with Earley et al. (1989) that the learning situation must facilitate the effective use of metacognitive or self-regulatory skills. A critical issue in the development and effective use of metacognitive skills is the opportunity for individuals to engage in self-directed learning. Learner control allows individuals to adjust the instruction to their own needs. However, individuals differ in their capability to take advantage of an environment in which they can structure their own learning (Dorner & Scholkopf, 1991; Etelapelto, 1993).

Research has generally examined the effects of metacognition in classroom settings. Several studies have found relationships between self-reported metacognitive activities and achievement outcomes. Pintrich and De-Groot (1990) found that individual assessments of selfregulated learning were positively related to academic performance. Pokay and Blumenfeld (1990) found that self-reported metacognition was negatively related to achievement early in the semester, but positively related to achievement at the end of the semester. Meloth (1990) found that explicit instruction on knowledge of cognition led to an improvement of participants' knowledge of cognition and that this increase was associated with improved strategy use and comprehension performance. Volet (1991) found that computer students taught metacognitive activities received better course grades and were better at applying their knowledge to solving new problems.

The present study expands research on metacognition by examining the metacognitive processes of adult learners mastering a complex, decision-making task. In the present study, it is hypothesized that metacognitive activity will be positively related to the learning outcomes of knowledge and final training performance. Individuals who monitor their learning of the task, identify errors in performance, and adjust their learning activities should acquire more knowledge about the task and develop more effective procedures for performing the task.

The relationship between metacognitive activity and self-efficacy may be more complex. One might expect that more metacognitive activity will lead to the development of greater self-efficacy. However, the positive or negative feedback an individual generates through metacognitive activity may determine the actual influence on his or her self-efficacy (Schunk, 1990). Because this study focuses only on the amount of metacognitive activity, we expect a low to moderate relationship between metacognitive activity and self-efficacy.

Research on learning strategies has focused on how to teach individuals effective methods for learning various types of text-based information (e.g., Collins, Dansereau, Garland, Holley, & McDonald, 1981; Dansereau, 1978, 1985). Little or no research has focused on which learning strategies are effective for acquiring skills in cognitively complex, dynamic tasks. In the present study, we are interested in how individuals take advantage of the opportunity to control some portions of their learning.

Trainers have long relied on the theory of identical elements as a guide to design training that maximizes transfer (Royer, 1979). Identical elements theory states that transfer from one task to another is greater the more elements that are shared between the two tasks (Osgood, 1949; Thorndike & Woodworth, 1901). More recent research has determined that it is the similarity of the information processing between the training and transfer tasks that is most important (Bransford & Franks, 1976; Lung & Dominowski, 1985). The training exercises presented to individuals in this study vary in their level of complexity; this dictates how similar each training scenario is to the high-complexity transfer task. Individuals in this study were allowed to choose practice exercises that range from low to high complexity. Lower complexity exercises isolate task components or present them in simpler forms, or both. Higher complexity scenarios present integrated task components in more complex forms. Individuals were told that the most complex training scenario is the closest to what they will experience in the transfer task.
Given a choice, some individuals may attempt to max-

imize practice task similarity to the transfer task. Therefore, one possible strategy for learning would be to practice the most complex training exercise as often as possible. We label this as high on the identical elements strategy continuum as the purpose is to familiarize oneself with the demands of the transfer task. In contrast, individuals may use a strategy of practicing the less complex scenarios and building up to the more complex scenarios. Individuals might choose this part—whole or task variability (Goldstein, 1993) strategy because they believe it will enable them to gain a potentially deeper understanding of the task, to examine different relationships among task elements, or to understand the effects of different combinations of the task elements. This represents a strategy that is low on the identical elements continuum as individuals are choosing to practice a greater number of training scenarios that vary in terms of complexity.

Figure 1 presents hypothesized links between the identical elements practice strategy and the three learning outcomes of knowledge, final training performance, and selfefficacy. Being exposed to the integrated demands of the most complex training scenario is expected to be the best preparation for performance on the transfer task, by providing individuals with greater knowledge, skill proficiency, and self-efficacy at the end of training. For a complex task, acquiring strategies to deal with task components in isolation may be difficult to integrate for the whole task (Gopher, Weil, & Siegel, 1989). Thus, using a ramping strategy from low to high complexity may not allow the trainee enough practice to be prepared to generalize their knowledge and skills to the additional complexity included in the transfer task. By using an identical elements strategy, individuals will learn how the task operates as a whole. In addition, the more frequently the learner practices dealing with the most complex training scenario, the greater the individual's self-efficacy should be for handling the transfer task.

A second strategy concerns whether individuals spend their time practicing the skills that are important for task performance. Research on transfer has identified the opportunity to perform trained tasks as an important factor in training transfer (Ford, Quinones, Sego, & Sorra, 1992; Quinones et al., 1995). In the present study, we are interested in whether learners take advantage of the opportunity to practice skills mentioned as important for transfer during training. Activity level, or the number of times the individual practices key task skills, is identified as an important method for learning about the task. Individuals in this study can acquire two skills that will facilitate task performance. To successfully acquire these skills, learners must spend time assessing and acting on key pieces of information. This information will assist them in evaluating the task situation, developing effective strategies, and performing the task in an effective way.

It is hypothesized that the learner's activity level relevant to key task skills will be positively related to task knowledge, final training performance, and self-efficacy. By spending more time practicing the key task components of assessing and evaluating key pieces of information, individuals should develop an understanding of the deeper, structural features of the task (Newell, Rosenbloom, & Laird, 1989). Frequent practice should lead to greater proceduralization of these skills and better performance by the end of training (Rogers, Maurer, Salas. & Fisk, 1997). Finally, practice and mastery experiences are important for the development of self-efficacy (Bandura, 1982); therefore, the greater their activity level during training, the more confident learners should be in their capabilities to perform well on the transfer task. The next section describes individual differences in goal orientation and how these differences impact on metacognitive activity and practice strategies.

Researchers have long recognized the role of individual differences in learning and transfer. Learners differ in what they do during learning and in their capability to succeed in particular types of learning situations (Snow, 1989). For example, researchers have examined the impact of cognitive ability on the learning of complex skills (Kanfer & Ackerman, 1989) as well as the impact of trainee attitudes and motivation on learning and transfer outcomes (Noe & Schmitt, 1986; Tannenbaum, Mathieu, Salas, & Cannon-Bowers, 1991). In this study, we are particularly interested in motivational factors that operate under learner control conditions.

An individual difference construct of interest in current instructional and educational research is the goal orientation of the learner. Two types of goal orientations to achievement-related activities have been identified: mastery (or learning) orientation and performance orientation (Dweck, 1986). Mastery and performance orientations to learning represent different ideas of success and different reasons for engaging in learning (Ames, 1992).

A mastery orientation includes the belief that effort leads to improvement in outcomes and that ability is malleable. Individuals with a mastery orientation are focused on developing new skills, attempting to understand their tasks, and successfully achieving self-referenced standards for mastery. In contrast, individuals with a performance orientation to learning believe that ability is demonstrated by performing better than others, by surpassing normative-based standards, or by succeeding with little effort (Ames, 1992; Dweck, 1986). Individuals with a performance orientation want to publicly achieve greater success compared with others.
Research has found that classroom settings emphasiz-

ing mastery goals lead students to use more effective learning strategies, to prefer challenging tasks, to have a more positive attitude toward the class, and to have a stronger belief that success follows from effort. In contrast, classrooms emphasizing performance goals lead students to focus on their ability, to evaluate their ability negatively, and to attribute their failures to lack of ability (Ames & Archer, 1988). In addition, research shows that mastery goals lead to greater persistence in the face of difficulties, whereas performance goals led to the avoidance of challenging tasks (Dweck, 1986; Dweck & Leggett, 1988; Elliott & Dweck, 1988). Thus, some research indicates that the goal orientation of the learning setting can have an impact on individuals' learning activities.

Research has also tried to understand goal orientation as a more stable construct. Duda and Nicholls (1992) provided evidence that mastery and performance orientations are related to different personal beliefs. Performance orientation is related to the belief that success requires high ability, whereas mastery orientation is related to the belief that success requires interest, effort, and collaboration. Kroll (1988) found that mastery orientation is positively related to tolerance for ambiguity, thoughtfulness, and open-mindedness. Performance orientation is negatively related to tolerance for ambiguity, thoughtfulness, complexity, and individualism.

Researchers have considered whether mastery and performance orientation are two ends of a single construct or two separate constructs. Whereas some, such as Dweck (1986), seem to describe the two orientations as ends of a continuum, evidence suggests that they are two separate dimensions (Farr, Hofmann, & Ringenbach, 1993). Subsequent research has supported the construct validity of mastery and performance orientation as distinct constructs (Button, Mathieu, & Zajac, 1996; Phillips & Gully, in press). In the present study, it is expected that mastery orientation and performance orientation will be independent constructs. In addition, it is expected that mastery orientation will be the more critical factor to consider in a training environment in which individuals have some control over their learning activities. The beliefs that effort will lead to greater learning and that ability can in fact be improved should provide a greater foundation for individuals who are faced with the challenge of choosing their own training activities.

As shown in Figure 1, it is expected that mastery and performance orientations will have differential relationships with the learning strategies used during training. Individuals with a mastery orientation use deep processing strategies that require cognitive effort but lead to understanding; in contrast, performance orientation is related to more short-term and surface-level processing strategies (Meece, 1994). Therefore, it is hypothesized that the mastery orientation of the learner will be positively related to

metacognitive activity. In contrast, it is expected that a performance orientation will be negatively related to metacognitive activity. Those individuals whose goal it is to perform better than others will be focused on performing the task quickly and efficiently and will, thus, take a more shallow approach to learning.

Mastery and performance orientations should also be linked to the use of the identical elements strategy. Specifically, mastery orientation is hypothesized to be negatively related to identical elements. Individuals with a higher mastery orientation are focused on learning skills and understanding the nature of the task. They are more likely to explore the various aspects of the task both by choosing exercises that break it down into components and by trying to perform the task at different levels of complexity. In contrast, a performance orientation is hypothesized to be positively related to identical elements. Individuals with a performance orientation want to succeed in comparison with others, and the test of their success will be their performance on the transfer task. Therefore, they will be more likely to focus their attention on performing a training exercise that is most similar to the transfer task.

It is also hypothesized that a mastery orientation will be positively related to activity level. Mastery oriented individuals want to develop a rich understanding of task procedures, so they are more likely to practice important task skills as often as possible. In contrast, performanceoriented individuals are likely to show less persistence while performing a task (Dweck, 1986). Therefore, performance orientation is not expected to be related to activity level.

To summarize, Figure 1 presents the expected linkages among goal orientation, learning strategies, learning outcomes, and training transfer. We have generated a number of hypotheses regarding these linkages. The hypotheses are tested within the framework of a complex decisionmaking training program. The design of this training program allows the learner to have control over the learning process.

Participants were 93 undergraduate students enrolled in psychology courses at a large midwestern university. The participants were given class credit for participating in the study. In addition, participants had a chance to win a $40 cash prize awarded randomly to one of the participants in the top 25% of performers on the transfer task.

A total of 106 students participated in the study. The present study was based on the 93 participants who chose to practice the most complex training scenario for the last training trial. This allowed for a measure of skill proficiency at the end of training across a common scenario.

The task was a revised version of TANDEM (Tactical Naval Decision Making System; Dwyer, Hall, Volpe, Cannon-Bowers, & Salas, 1992). TANDEM is a PC-based, dynamic decisionmaking program that simulates a naval radar tracking task. This task has previously been used in research examining teamwork stressors (Inzana, Driskell, Salas, & Johnston, 1996; Weaver, Bowers, Salas, & Cannon-Bowers, 1995; Weaver, Morgan, Hall, & Compton, 1993). TANDEM presents trainees with multiple targets on the computer screen. Trainees are placed in the role of radar operator of a U.S. Navy missile cruiser. The operator is to ' 'hook'' a target on the radar screen and then collect information to classify the target's type, class, and intent. Then the operator must decide to shoot hostile targets and clear peaceful targets from the screen. The goal of the task is to correctly identify and process each target in the shortest amount of time possible. Individuals in this study learned how to deal with ambiguous information concerning target classifications as well as zones surrounding their ship in which targets were not allowed to enter. First, individuals were presented with certain information cues that conflicted with the information from the remaining cues used to make a classification. Individuals had to learn how to deal with this cue ambiguity when making classification decisions. In addition, individuals learned how to prevent targets from entering critical zones surrounding their own ship. If individuals allowed targets into these penalty circles, they would lose points. The optimal task strategy was to check the speed and range information for targets near the penalty circles in order to prioritize the targets that should be engaged first.

The training program was set up to allow trainees to control the types of scenarios they wanted to practice in order to prepare themselves for the transfer task. The content of the training program and the instructions on how the task was to be completed were provided by the experimenter.

Participants attended training on 2 consecutive days. The individual difference measures of mastery orientation and performance orientation were collected at the beginning of the 1st day. The 1st day also included training on the basic procedures for using the software and performing the task. Participants learned how to hook targets on the radar screen, how to pull down menus on the screen to access information about the targets, and how to zoom in and out on the radar screen to look for targets outside of the current viewing range.

Individuals made four decisions about each target they prosecuted. The first three decisions classified the type, class, and intent of each target. For the type decision, participants had to classify the target as air, surface, or submarine. For the class decision, they classified the target as civilian or military. For the intent decision, they classified the target as peaceful or hostile. For each of these three decisions, participants had to access five information cues and determine their value. Individuals used a table of information values to make these decisions.
In addition, participants had to make an engage decision by choosing whether to shoot a target or clear it from the screen.

The engage decision was dependent on the intent decision. If the intent was classified as hostile, the target should be shot. If the intent was classified as peaceful, the target should be cleared from the screen. Individuals could receive feedback on their decisions by holding down the mouse button after making the engage decision. This feedback indicated the points gained or lost and the correct type, class, and intent classifications for the target. Participants first watched the experimenter demonstrate how to perform the basic task procedures. Next, they read a description of the task and its procedures. Participants were then given a 5-min and a 10-min trial to perform the task themselves.

On the 2nd day the focus was on the portion of training in which the learners had control over the learning process. Participants first performed a 5-min trial to refamiliarize themselves with the basic procedures for performing the task that was taught on the previous day. Next, they were taught about two new task components that they would be given an opportunity to practice. The first task component was cue ambiguity. Cue ambiguity referred to the presence of one or two cues that conflict with the remainder of the five information cues necessary to make each of the type, class, and intent decisions about a target. Individuals were able to practice dealing with cue ambiguity at three levels of complexity. For the low level of cue ambiguity, one cue in the type decision was in conflict with the remaining information cues (e.g., the altitude indicated an air target, whereas the remaining cues indicated a submarine). For the medium level of complexity, one cue was in conflict for each of the three decisions, type, class, and intent. For the high level of complexity, two cues for each decision were in conflict with the remaining three cues. Individuals were instructed that the three consistent cues indicated the correct decision to be made.

The second task component that individuals learned was penalty circles. Penalty circles referred to the presence of one or more circles around the participants' ship that they were to defend and prevent targets from entering. If targets entered these zones, participants would lose points. This task component could also be practiced at a low, medium, or high level of complexity. For the low level of complexity, there was one penalty circle visible on the radar screen at 10 nautical miles (nm) that would cost 50 points if a target entered it. In the medium level of complexity, there were two penalty circles. The first circle was visible at 10 nni. The second penalty circle was not marked on the screen but was located at 128 nm. Each penalty circle cost 50 points if a target entered it. For the high level of complexity, there were the two penalty circles described previously. However, the outer penalty circle cost 100 points if a target entered it. In the high level of complexity, participants had to learn the counterintuitive skill of focusing on the penalty circle farther from their own ship as the one that was more costly.

Individuals were given the opportunity to practice cue ambiguity and penalty circles at low, medium, and high levels of complexity. Scenarios were developed that allowed for the practice of these two task components alone and in combination. A total of 15 scenarios were created. Participants were presented a matrix on their computer screen that allowed them to choose which scenarios to practice, in the order they preferred, during training. In addition, they were provided a matrix sheet that

described the components of each scenario. Individuals were told that the most complex training scenario, which included cue ambiguity and penalty circles at high levels of complexity, was the closest to what they would experience on the transfer task.

Participants were given twelve 5-min practice trials to prepare themselves for the transfer task. They were told not to worry about their score during the training scenarios, but instead to use this information to learn about the task. After the 12 practice trials, participants completed measures of metacognitive activity and self-efficacy and completed a knowledge test. After a 5 min break, individuals were presented with a 12-min transfer task that was more difficult than the training scenarios they had practiced.

Mastery orientation. Participants completed an eight-item scale developed by Button et al. (1996). A sample item was "The opportunity to learn new things is important to me." Individuals responded on a 5-point scale ranging from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5). Coefficient alpha for the scale was .79.

Performance orientation. Participants completed an eightitem scale developed by Button et al. (1996). A sample item was "I feel smart when I do something without making any mistakes." Individuals responded on a 5-point scale ranging from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5). Coefficient alpha for the scale was .76.

Identical elements. Identical elements was indexed by the number of times the individual practiced the scenario most similar to the transfer task. Although the transfer task was not identical to the most complex practice task, it did include the same level of complexity for cue ambiguity and penalty circles. Key differences in the transfer task were the inclusion of multiple pop-up targets, the additional time to perform, and the greater number of targets close to the penalty circles. The identical element index could range from 1 to 12.

Activity level. The activity level index assessed how frequently individuals practiced an important task strategy for classifying targets and for prioritizing the targets they should engage during the exercise. An effective task strategy to learn was checking the speed and range values for each target. First, this information helped to classify the target's type. Second, this strategy allowed individuals to prevent targets that were traveling fast and were close in range from entering the penalty circles. An index was computed to assess the average number of times individuals accessed the speed and range information during the first 11 trials: number of speed queries + number of range queries/number of targets engaged. Practice of this strategy for the 12th training trial was not included in the index because the 12th trial was used as a measure of final training performance.

Metacognitive activity. Participants completed a 12-item scale at the end of training to assess the extent to which they engaged in metacognitive activity during the training session. Items were developed to assess self-monitoring of learning, choice of scenarios to practice in order to address difficulties or problems, and self-evaluation of one's progress. An example item was "I noticed where I made the most mistakes during

practice and focused on improving those areas." Participants rated their metacognition on a 5-point scale ranging from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5). Coefficient alpha for the scale was .83.

Knowledge test. A nine-item multiple-choice test was developed to assess participants' knowledge of different aspects of the task. Several items tapped declarative knowledge about the information cues used to make decisions. In addition, items were written to assess strategic knowledge of the most efficient way to access information cues under conditions of ambiguity and how to prioritize targets to deal with the presence of two penalty circles. Participants completed the knowledge test at the end of training. Alpha for this test was .59.

Training performance. Training performance was assessed by the score achieved on the 12th training trial. The score was based on two aspects of the task. First, individuals would gain 100 points for each target for which they made all four decisions correct (i.e., type, class, intent, and engage). They would lose 100 points if any of the four decisions was incorrect. In addition, participants would lose 50 points for any target allowed to enter the inner penalty circle and would lose 100 points for any target allowed to enter the outer penalty circle.

Self-efficacy. Individuals completed an eight-item scale to assess their confidence in their ability to perform successfully on this task. An example item was "I can meet the challenges of this simulation." Participants rated their self-efficacy on a 5-point scale ranging from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5). Participants completed this scale at the end of training. Coefficient alpha for this scale was .90.

Transfer performance. Participants performed a final 12-min scenario at the end of the 2nd day of the experiment. This scenario was more difficult than the training scenarios. The transfer scenario was longer in duration (12 min vs. 5 min), and it included more targets on the screen (33 vs. 12) and a greater number of targets that popped up suddenly on the screen. Also, a greater proportion of targets surrounded the outer, more costly, penalty circle. In addition, participants no longer had any written materials to help them perform the task. Specifically, they no longer had the table that matched values for the information cues to the classification decisions. Transfer score was based on the same point values used in the final training scenario: 100 points gained for all correct decisions or 100 points lost for at
least one incorrect decision per target, and 50 points for inner penalty circle intrusions and 100 points for outer penalty circle intrusions.

Figure 1 depicts a path model in which individual difference factors are related to learning strategies used during training, which then are related to learning outcomes. Finally, learning outcomes are related to training transfer. Relationships between specific variables in this model are hypothesized. However, these bivariate hypotheses must be tested within the overall conceptual model to provide a stringent test of these relationships. Therefore, hierarchical regression analysis was chosen as the dataanalytic strategy for testing the conceptual model (Cohen & Cohen, 1983; Pedhazur, 1982). Variables were entered into the regression equation on the basis of their temporal ordering in the model. All variables occurring prior to or at the same point in the conceptual model are controlled for in the regression analysis before examining bivariate relationships. This provides a rigorous examination of the specific hypotheses that comprise the overall conceptual model.

Table 1 presents the means, standard deviations, reliabilities, and intercorrelations of the variables in the study. Results supported the hypothesis that mastery and performance orientation are separate constructs. As expected, mastery orientation and performance orientation were not significantly correlated and were differentially related to several constructs, such as metacognition, self-efficacy, and transfer performance.

The second set of analyses focused on the influence of goal orientation and learning strategies on the three learning outcomes. The final set of analyses examined the impact of goal orientation, learning strategies, and learning outcomes on transfer performance.

This study examined a model of how goal orientation, metacognitive activity, and practice strategies are related to multiple learning outcomes and transfer within a training environment in which individuals were able to choose their own practice exercises. The results of regression analyses supported many of the specific links in the model.
In particular, support was found for a key path of rela-tionships from mastery orientation to subsequent meta-cognitive activity during training. The extensiveness of

metacognitive activity was significantly related to knowledge and skill acquisition as well as to perceptions of self-efficacy. In turn, the three learning outcomes were all found to be significant factors predicting performance in a more complex transfer task. In terms of the practice strategies, the identical elements strategy was related to perceptions of self-efficacy, whereas the activity level variable was related to knowledge and final training performance. Goal orientation, though, was not related to the two practice strategies. Finally, correlational results supported the distinction of mastery and performance orientation as two separate constructs (Button et al., 1996). The two goal orientations were unrelated to one another and were differentially related to several other constructs in this study.

We believe that there are at least four key findings from this study with implications for future research. First, the significant results linking the three learning outcomes and transfer performance support the need for a multidimensional perspective to learning outcomes (Kraiger et al., 1993). Each learning outcome predicted transfer performance, even though the analyses required that variance due to the other two learning outcomes were controlled when testing the impact of the third or focal learning outcome on transfer performance. At first glance the significant relationship between knowledge acquisition and transfer performance would seem to be at odds with the training evaluation meta-analytic reviews by Alliger and his colleagues (Alliger & Janak, 1989; Alliger, Tannenbaum, Bennett, Traver, & Shetland, 1997). They found

little relationship between learning measures and behavioral transfer measures. We believe these meta-analytic results are due to the difficulty of developing specific, high-quality measures of learning and transfer in field studies. Our findings are more consistent with selection validation meta-analytic work conducted with much larger samples (e.g.. Hunter, 1983; Ree, Carretta, & Teachout, 1995; F. L. Schmidt, Hunter, & Outerbridge, 1986). These studies, for example, have consistently found that job knowledge has a strong, positive relationship with work sample performance (which is similar to our measure of transfer). Our findings support the need to examine knowledge, skill, and affective outcomes of learning on transfer performance.

Second, the results for self-efficacy are important in showing that training researchers need to consider the role of affective and motivational learning outcomes, in addition to knowledge and skills, in the transfer of training (Kraiger et al., 1993). In our study, the motivational relationship between self-efficacy and transfer performance was evident even after controlling for the level of knowledge and skill obtained. We contend that this motivational effect is related to resilience (Bandura & Wood, 1989). This suggests that individuals high on self-efficacy were more resilient in the face of greater task complexity.

Third, the results of our study also indicate that learning strategies were related to these multiple learning outcomes. Metacognitive activity was the most important strategy, in that it was related to all three learning outcomes. Individuals who monitored their learning, tried to

diagnose where they were having difficulties, and adjusted their behavior accordingly developed greater knowledge of the task, better performance strategies, and greater confidence in their task capabilities. These learning capabilities then led to greater performance on the transfer task. These results support the research by Earley et al. (1989) and others that focused on the importance of self-regulatory activities such as effective strategy selection and implementation. Self-regulatory activities such as metacognition can lead to effective learning early in the knowledge and skill acquisition process if trainees are provided with a learning environment that places greater emphasis on acquiring and mastering skills than on performing well on outcome measures during training.

Fourth, this study also supports recent calls for examining the influence of mastery orientation and performance orientation on learning outcomes (Button et al., 1996). Individuals with a higher mastery orientation engaged in greater metacognitive activity during learning. Results showed that mastery orientation was related to learning through the more general, executive-level strategy of metacognition rather than through any specific practice strategies used during training. Individuals who approached learning environments with the purpose of mastering new things were more active in attending to and correcting their understanding of the task. In addition, metacognition was found to partially mediate the relationship between mastery orientation and self-efficacy. Mastery orientation also had a direct, positive relationship with self-efficacy after controlling for learning strategies. Performance orientation was not related to learning strategies, but it did have some relationships with learning outcomes and transfer. Results indicated a mediated path from performance orientation to self-efficacy to transfer performance. Individuals with a higher performance orientation were less self-efficacious at the end of training, and this was related to their poorer performance on the transfer task. Given that trainees were not provided with normative feedback during training, performance-oriented individuals may have felt less confident prior to completing the transfer task.

A strength of the study was the use of multiple learning outcomes that were cognitive, skill-based, and affective. Researchers should continue to examine these multiple outcomes, using different conceptualizations of knowledge, skill, and affect. This study included a measure of transfer to examine how learning outcomes related to performance on a more difficult version of the task. Although the transfer task posed certain difficulties, it required trainees to use and apply their knowledge and skills from training. This conceptualization of transfer is consis-

tent with the notion of near transfer, in which the stimulus complexity of the training and transfer tasks are similar and require the same response (Royer, 1979). Researchers have also been interested in far transfer, in which individuals adapt their knowledge and skills to a task that differs in stimulus features from the training task. A fruitful area for research would be to examine how individual motivational factors, learning strategies, and metacognition influence adaptation to a far transfer task. In this way, we can begin to identify training design principles (e.g., how to improve metacognitive activity) that may have an impact not only on knowledge and skill acquisition, but also on training transfer (R. A. Schmidt & Bjork, 1992).

Unexpected results in this study were the direct relationships between mastery orientation and performance orientation and self-efficacy after controlling for learning strategies and metacognition. Metacognition did provide some mediation for the relationship between mastery orientation and self-efficacy. However, there may be other learning strategies or activities that might be mediators. Future research should consider additional conceptualizations of learning strategies to better understand how goal orientation affects the process of building self-efficacy during learning. In addition, an individual's perception of self-efficacy is likely to change as one proceeds through the practice trials. Tracking this dynamic process was beyond the scope of the present research. Nevertheless, future research is needed to examine the changing nature of relationships between learning strategies and self-efficacy perceptions.

In addition, this study found that identical elements and activity level practice strategies were positively related to learning outcomes. However, mastery orientation and performance orientation did not influence the use of these strategies. Researchers should examine other individual difference factors that might predict these learning strategies. For example, learning style is a predisposition to adopt a particular learning strategy, regardless of the specific demands of the learning task (Schmeck, 1983). Schmeck identified four major categories of learning styles: (a) deep processing, (b) methodical study, (c) elaborative processing, and (d) fact retention. These types of individual differences may be important influences on the extent to which individuals adopt specific learning strategies while practicing the task.

An interesting result of the study was the positive relationship between metacognition and self-efficacy. It was not expected that a strong relationship would be found, because we did not know whether the self-evaluations resulting from metacognition were positive or negative. Nonetheless, engaging in greater metacognitive activity was related to greater self-confidence in the learner's capability to succeed at the task. Future research should examine not only metacognitive activity but also how spe-
cific self-evaluations lead to adjustments during learning and subsequent learning outcomes.

This study measured metacognition as a summary perception at the end of training. This may be a limitation of the study, as some researchers have questioned whether individuals can accurately report their use of metacognitive strategies. However, Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons (1988) provided some evidence for the construct validity of self-reported metacognition. They found that students' reports of self-regulatory learning strategies correlated .70 with teachers' ratings of their self-regulation. Nonetheless, this study was a first step in trying to understand the role of metacognition when individuals are responsible for their own learning. Future research can measure metacognition during training by asking certain questions as individuals are learning and processing the task. Verbal protocol analysis has been identified as one way to try to measure metacognition more immediately and directly (Kraiger et al., 1993). In addition, this study focused on the amount of metacognitive activity; however, an important consideration for future research would be the accuracy of metacognitive monitoring and evaluation and how this accuracy affects learning and transfer.

It should also be noted that the identical elements strategy was defined in a particular way in this study. Identical elements was based on the practice of the most complex training exercise that most closely resembled the highly complex transfer task. Thus, identical elements is defined in terms of high task complexity in this study. Future research should disentangle task complexity from the identical elements strategy.

This study examined one type of learning environment, in which individuals were able to choose their own practice exercises. This environment was selected so we could examine how learners direct their own learning activities. Future research should compare both traditional training environments, and environments that allow more learner control, to understand what individual factors and learning strategies are important in each of these settings.

This study examined one possible conceptualization of how individual differences and learning activities are related to learning outcomes and transfer. However, it is reasonable to expect that the learning process is more complex than the preliminary model tested in this study. For example, there may be interacting influences between general metacognitive activity and the specific learning strategies used by individuals. A particular learning strategy may be effective if individuals are engaged in active monitoring and evaluation, whereas it may prove ineffective if it were carried out without conscious reflection and diagnosis. In addition, individuals who engage in metacognition are likely to change their specific practice strategies as they monitor what they have learned over time.
Future research should examine how these learning strategies interact and relate during learning.

Finally, this study did not use a true experimental design, as participants were not randomly assigned to condition (e.g., high or low on the identical elements strategy). Although our conceptual framework and the temporal ordering of variables might allow for the suggestion of causality (Cook & Campbell, 1979), we have been careful to avoid the use of causal language in this article. A stronger, experimental design might therefore be useful for more fully exploring the relationships investigated in this study. In the absence of an experimental design, additional research is needed to allow for the cross-validation of the results found in the present study.

The findings from the study begin to suggest a number of principles for designing and delivering effective training interventions for enhancing performance in complex environments. First, as has been suggested, training is more than just providing knowledge and skills to trainees (Kraiger et al., 1993). This study shows that a broader view of training is needed that includes (and values) affective outcomes. Therefore, instructional developers should incorporate into training specific learning events that facilitate the development of self-efficacy and other motivational outcomes. This is important because selfefficacy may provide a resiliency to any difficulties faced in trying to apply what was learned back to the work setting. For example, this study showed a positive relationship between metacognitive activity during training and self-efficacy at the end of training. Explicit instruction or guidance on metacognitive activity may be one way to facilitate the development of self-efficacy.

Second, trainee motivation has been shown to be critical in the success of training programs (Noe & Schmitt, 1986; Tannenbaum et al., 1991). This study adds to that body of knowledge by suggesting that efforts to improve trainee motivation during training (i.e., allowing for mastery goals) may lead to better transfer. Therefore, instructional designers should deliver training interventions embedded with mastery goal oriented learning objectives. This would create a flexible and adaptable learning environment—conditions that are critical for enhancing complex decision-making performance in dynamic tasks such as military command and control situations.

Finally, the nature of practice is not well understood (Salas, Cannon-Bowers, & Kozlowski, 1997). This study begins to suggest that all practice is not equal. The activities that trainees engage in to direct their own learning are crucial for skill acquisition. Therefore, instructional developers should create methods to aid instructors to guide and structure the learning experience. For example,

the designer can consider certain stages in the training intervention in which they can give trainees more or less guidance. Future research is needed to validate these principles. However, this study provides theoretically based insights for designing training to enhance performance in cognitively complex, dynamic environments.
